title: Forecasting in Brief
text:
Preface
This short book introduces a few ideas from time series forecasting. It is also a working demonstration of quarto-i18n, a Quarto extension that keeps machine translations of a book in step with its English source.
The author writes only the English chapters. Every other language is generated by a translator, checked by the tool, and then improved by readers who review paragraphs and suggest better wording.






TipTry it



Switch to Français or Español in the sidebar, then choose Review this page in the notice at the top of a chapter. Each paragraph shows how many people have reviewed its translation.


The material follows the approach of Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), which is freely available online.




Hyndman, Rob J., and George Athanasopoulos. 2021. Forecasting: Principles and Practice. 3rd ed. OTexts. https://otexts.com/fpp3/.

title: 1  Time series data
text:
1.1 What makes a series special
A time series is a sequence of observations of the same quantity, recorded at regular intervals. Monthly airline passenger numbers, daily electricity demand, weekly retail sales and quarterly unemployment rates are all time series.
Unlike most data sets, the order of the observations matters. Each value is related to the values before it, and a forecast uses that relationship to say something about the future.
Three features appear again and again:

title: 1  Time series data
text:
A trend is a long-term increase or decrease in the data.
Seasonality is a pattern that repeats with a fixed period, such as every year or every week.
A cycle rises and falls without a fixed period, often over several years.

title: 1  Time series data
text:
1.2 The data in this book
Most examples use AirPassengers, a classic data set that ships with R. It records the number of international airline passengers each month from 1949 to 1960, in thousands. The series has {r} length(AirPassengers) observations.1






NoteFrequency



The frequency of a series is the number of observations in one seasonal period. Monthly data have a frequency of 12.

title: 1  Time series data
text: The data were published by Box and Jenkins and are often used to illustrate multiplicative seasonality.↩︎

title: 2  Visualising a time series
text:
2.1 Seasonal plots
The first step in any forecasting task is to plot the data. A time plot shows the observations against time and makes the trend and seasonality easy to see.
Figure 2.1 shows a clear upward trend. The seasonal pattern also grows with the level of the series: the summer peaks become larger every year.
A seasonal plot draws each year as a separate line, so that the shape of the seasonal pattern is easier to compare from one year to the next.
# One line per year, coloured from earliest to latest
passengers$year <- format(passengers$month, "%Y")
passengers$month_of_year <- as.integer(format(passengers$month, "%m"))

ggplot(passengers, aes(x = month_of_year, y = count, group = year, colour = year)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(x = "Month of the year", y = "Passengers (thousands)", colour = "Year")







Figure 2.2: Each year of the series drawn as its own line.
July and August are the busiest months in every year of the data.

title: 3  Simple forecasting methods
text:
3.1 Naive and seasonal naive
Some forecasting methods are extremely simple and yet surprisingly effective. They are mostly used as benchmark methods: any new method should do better than these before it is worth using.
The naive method uses the last observation as the forecast for every future period. The seasonal naive method instead uses the value from the same season of the last year, so a forecast for next July is this July’s value.
h <- 24  # forecast horizon in months
last_year <- tail(as.numeric(AirPassengers), 12)

# Repeat the final year of data to cover the horizon
forecast_values <- rep(last_year, length.out = h)
future <- seq(as.Date("1961-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = h)

message(sprintf("Produced %d forecasts from %d observations", h, length(AirPassengers)))

Produced 24 forecasts from 144 observations

plot(future, forecast_values, type = "l",
     main = "Seasonal naive forecasts",
     xlab = "Month", ylab = "Passengers (thousands)")







Figure 3.1: Seasonal naive forecasts for the next two years.
Because the series has a strong trend, the seasonal naive forecasts in Figure 3.1 are probably too low. A method that also models the trend would do better.

title: 3  Simple forecasting methods
text:
3.2 Measuring uncertainty
A single number hides how uncertain a forecast is. A prediction interval gives a range in which the future value is expected to lie with a stated probability, such as 80% or 95%. Intervals usually become wider as the forecast horizon increases, because uncertainty accumulates over time.

title: 4  How this book is translated
text:
4.1 One source, many languages
This chapter describes what happens between the English source and the translated pages you can read in the other languages.
The author edits only the English .qmd files and _quarto.yml. Each translated language lives in a set of translation files under _i18n/, one file per chapter. Every paragraph, caption and code comment is a separate unit with its own source text, translation and list of reviewers.

title: 4  How this book is translated
text:
4.2 Translating
Running i18n translate collects the units that are new or whose English text has changed. A translator fills them in, and the tool checks every result before it is accepted. Inline code, links, citations, cross-references and shortcodes must come back unchanged, and translated code must parse with R’s own parser.
crumbs: 4  How this book is translated

title: 4  How this book is translated
text:
4.3 Keeping translations honest
When a paragraph changes in English, its translation becomes stale. Readers then see the English paragraph, marked as such, until the unit is translated again. A translation is never silently wrong.
In code cells, only comments and display strings such as plot titles are translated. Variable names and data never change, so every language runs the same analysis. If a translated cell fails, the build uses the English cell.

4.4 Reviewing
Choose Review this page in the notice to turn on reviewer mode. Each paragraph is marked by the number of people who have reviewed it. Select a paragraph to see the English source, then approve the translation or suggest a better one. Your changes are collected and submitted together as a pull request.
